summary: Prefetch coordination timeout causing gradual throughput decay in dedicated pool
description:
Issue summary:
Customer (NimbusDocs, dedicated) reported a slow, progressive throughput degradation in their reserved GPU pool over ~90 minutes. P50 stayed stable but p95/p99 and overall completed requests / second trended downward while queue length and batch serialization increased. No large traffic spike from the customer. This ticket collects the operational investigation, telemetry excerpts, mitigation steps, and next actions.

Observed behavior:
- Gradual throughput decay (~20-40% reduction over 1.5 hours) starting at 2026-03-10T09:12:00Z.
- Concurrent rise in kv-prefetch pending queue length and prefetch_ack_latency (tail).
- Autoscaler observed transient CPU/memory signals, initiated small scale-up, then scaled down as signals stabilized causing slot churn.
- Several short-lived evictions and increased batch serialization (many tiny batches).

Why unique/different from prior tickets:
Pattern is not an instantaneous noisy-tenant flood but a coordination timeout between prefetch subsystem and allocator/sidecar that slowly reduces effective throughput as batches serialize and allocator misinterprets heartbeats as slots released. Existing issues cover classic noisy tenants and snapshot I/O — this one points to prefetch ack path timing and sidecar telemetry jitter as root contributors.
impact: Customer-facing requests experienced lower overall RPS and elevated tail latency (p99 up from ~230ms to ~1.1s). Several API calls returned 429-like throttling on client backpressure as their local queueing grew. Customer reported degraded user experience for their interactive summarization flow. Billing or invoicing unaffected.
timeline: 2026-03-10T09:12Z - first alert from internal throughput monitor. 09:18Z - customer reported via in-app ticket. 09:22Z - Support triaged and engaged SRE. 09:35Z - initial hypothesis: noisy tenant. 10:05Z - SRE observed kv-prefetch pending queue growth in cluster metrics. 10:40Z - temporary mitigation applied (increase autoscaler min allocation & raise prefetch timeout). 11:10Z - partial recovery in throughput; monitoring continues. 2026-03-12 - engineering patch for sidecar prefetch ACK race merged to main and scheduled for canary deploy.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Customer runs steady low-latency interactive workload (many short streaming requests) pinned to dedicated pool in us-west.
2) After ~30-90 minutes of normal traffic, observe kv-prefetch pending queue steadily grow in the tenant's shard metrics.
3) Scheduler begins issuing attach/detach cycles as it perceives slot churn; small batches increase in frequency and batch size drops.
4) Autoscaler sees transient signals (sidecar telemetry jitter) and scales up then down, causing additional slot churn.
5) End-to-end throughput declines and p99 latency increases without a single large noisy burst from other tenants.

metrics_snapshot: Key metric deltas during window (09:10-10:10Z): throughput RPS -30%, p99 latency +380%, kv-prefetch_pending +420%, attach/detach ops +250%.
investigation_notes: Checked historical baselines for the dedicated pool: no scheduled maintenance or hardware degradation events during window.
Correlated sidecar telemetry traces with allocator logs and found repeated prefetch ack latencies clustered around the same tenants/shards.
Heap/driver-level GPU errors were absent; GPU utilization remained within expected bounds, but effective batch packing dropped dramatically.
Autoscaler decision logs show a small scale up (reactive) followed by scale down when telemetry smoothing removed the spike — this oscillation amplified slot churn.
Can reproduce internal repro in staging by artificially injecting 400-700ms delays into prefetch_ack path which triggers similar attach/detach churn and throughput drop.
No customer-side SDK change; traffic patterns consistent with standard short-stream interactive usage.
Related telemetry points to a recent sidecar telemetry bump (v2.19.1) rolled out to a subset of nodes two days prior — timing and canary overlap with affected hosts.
hypothesis: Primary: A regression in sidecar telemetry/prefetch ACK handling introduced tail ack latency. This causes the allocator to interpret prefetch failures/timeouts as slot release or livelock, increasing attach/detach ops and creating many small batches (batch serialization).
Secondary: Autoscaler smoothing and aggressive scale-down combined with transient telemetry spikes to create a feedback loop that magnified throughput loss.
Tertiary: Edge cases in prefetch timeout configuration (short default) make dedicated pools with many short streams particularly sensitive.
mitigation: 1) Immediate: Increased autoscaler min capacity for NimbusDocs dedicated pool by +2 to reduce impact from transient scale-downs (applied 10:40Z).
2) Immediate: Raised prefetch_ack timeout from 250ms -> 1000ms in pool-level config for affected pool (temporary guardrail).
3) Short-term: Rolled back sidecar telemetry v2.19.1 on the small canary subset pending root cause analysis (decision at 10:55Z).
4) Medium-term: Engineering prepared a fix to make prefetch ack path resilient to delayed telemetry messages instead of timing out slot leases.

resolution: In-progress: Temporary config changes produced partial recovery. Engineering has merged a patch to the sidecar and runtime to avoid prefetch ACK races (PRs referenced above). Plan: canary rollout 2026-03-12 18:00Z -> region roll forward pending metrics. Follow-ups: add alert for prefetch_ack_latency > 500ms, tune autoscaler smoothing to avoid aggressive scale-down when prefetch_pending > threshold, and run a focused postmortem after full rollout.
next_actions: 1) Canary deploy sidecar/runtime patch to 5% hosts in us-west and monitor kv-prefetch_pending and attach/detach ops for 60m (owner: Miguel Santos).
2) Create a dedicated alert (SLO/monitoring) for sustained prefetch_ack_tail > 500ms and kv-prefetch_pending growth (owner: Observability team).
3) Revisit default prefetch timeout across dedicated pools and document recommended pool-level overrides for short-stream workloads (owner: Platform Product).
4) Postmortem write-up and customer-facing summary for NimbusDocs (owner: Support/Product).
